passage:
Varun: I've been thinking about the plot in Dehradun. I should get sixty percent. I'm the one who paid the tax all these years.
Pema: Sixty? Papa said equal. You know that.
Varun: Things changed. I've done more.
Pema: I'm honestly angry right now, so I'm not answering this at midnight.
Pema: Tomorrow I'm writing down what we each remember agreeing on. And I'd like Uncle Tashi to sit with us, since he knew what Papa wanted.
Varun: You don't trust me?
Pema: I trust you. That's why I want it on paper, so neither of us has to rely on memory. We're still family, whatever happens to the plot. 🤍
Varun: Fine. Send me the list.
Pema: It'll be there by morning.

qa.q: How much of the plot does Varun say should be theirs?
qa.a: Varun says sixty percent, since Varun paid the tax all these years.

qa.q: What is Pema feeling, and how does Pema handle it?
qa.a: Pema is angry and says so plainly, then decides not to answer at midnight.

qa.q: What steps does Pema take to stop the dispute wrecking the relationship?
qa.a: Pema writes down what each of them remembers agreeing on and asks Uncle Tashi, who knew what Papa wanted, to sit with them.

qa.q: How might Varun be hearing Pema's plan to put things on paper?
qa.a: Varun may hear it as distrust, which is why Varun asks 'You don't trust me?'; Pema's reply that paper protects both of them softens that.

grounding: Pema is angry about a sibling's push for more family land and answers by putting agreements in writing, involving a neutral elder and keeping the relationship.

passage: Himani, sit. I am Sarita, and you asked why I never fight with your Uncle Rohit over the house papers, so I'll tell you. When I was twenty-five, Amma and Baba bought Rohit a motorbike for passing one exam. My first-class degree got a sweet and a pat on the head. Then came the talk about the will, and Baba said, "Rohit will need more, he's a boy." I sat in the kitchen while my tea went cold, feeling like furniture. I could have shouted at Rohit. He hadn't asked for any of it. Instead, one evening I told Amma, quietly, "It hurts when my work goes unseen." She went silent, then said she hadn't realised. It didn't fix everything. But I stopped waiting for applause and took the evening course I'd wanted. Rohit and I still share Diwali dinners. That mattered more than winning an argument would have.

qa.q: What did Amma and Baba buy Rohit for passing one exam?
qa.a: They bought Rohit a motorbike.

qa.q: How did Sarita feel in the kitchen while the tea went cold?
qa.a: Sarita felt like furniture, unseen and hurt, yet did not blame Rohit, who hadn't asked for any of it.

qa.q: What did Sarita do instead of turning it into a fight with Rohit?
qa.a: Sarita told Amma quietly that it hurts when work goes unseen, took the evening course Sarita had wanted, and kept sharing Diwali dinners with Rohit.

qa.q: How might Amma have experienced Sarita's quiet words?
qa.a: Amma went silent and then said she hadn't realised, which suggests Amma had not noticed the hurt until it was said calmly.

grounding: An adult child feels unseen by parents who favour a sibling, says so calmly, avoids war with the sibling and builds worth through their own course.

passage:
Gopika: Did you sign the flat lease?
Arnab: Not yet. The landlord wants an answer today.
Gopika: Send me the agreement, I'll read it with you.
Arnab: I can read it myself, Gopika.
Gopika: I know. Sorry. I keep wanting to fix it for you 😅
Arnab: I'm the one who has to live there.
Gopika: True. What do you want me to do, if anything?
Arnab: Just be around if I get stuck. And tell me if the deposit sounds normal.
Gopika: That I can do. And whichever you pick, I'm behind you, even if I'd have chosen the other flat.
Arnab: Thanks. That actually helps 🙂

qa.q: What does the landlord want from Arnab today?
qa.a: The landlord wants an answer today about the flat.

qa.q: What does Gopika mean by 'I keep wanting to fix it for you'?
qa.a: Gopika feels a protective urge to take over and recognises it as steering rather than support.

qa.q: What could Gopika do to support Arnab without taking control?
qa.a: Stay around in case Arnab gets stuck and answer the questions Arnab asks, while accepting the choice belongs to Arnab even if Gopika would have picked the other flat.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel when Gopika offers to read the agreement?
qa.a: Arnab may feel treated as unable to cope, which explains 'I can read it myself'; Gopika's apology lets Arnab ask for help on Arnab's own terms. 🙂

grounding: An older sibling feels protective of a younger sibling starting out, offers support and listens, and accepts that the choices are the younger sibling's.

passage:
The power had gone out an hour ago, and Irawati was feeling around for a candle when the phone buzzed. It was Asif, calling from a station platform where the last train had been cancelled.

"I didn't get the job," Asif said. "And I'm not sure I wanted it."

Irawati sat down on the floor. Once, she would have said, "I told you to prepare more." Tonight she said, "That sounds like a heavy day. Tell me the part you're not sure about."

The line crackled. Asif talked about the interviewers, then about a fear of disappointing Ma. Irawati listened and asked one question, then another. "I won't tell Ma," she said. "Unless you want me to."

When the train finally came, Asif laughed. "Thanks for not bossing me." Irawati smiled in the dark, glad to be needed.

qa.q: Where was Asif calling from?
qa.a: Asif was calling from a station platform where the last train had been cancelled.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling as Asif talked?
qa.a: Irawati was glad to be needed, and the care she took to listen rather than lecture shows it.

qa.q: How did Irawati avoid slipping into the old bossy-elder role?
qa.a: Instead of saying 'I told you to prepare more,' Irawati said the day sounded heavy, asked questions, and promised not to tell Ma unless Asif wanted her to.

qa.q: What might Asif have wanted from Irawati that night?
qa.a: Asif seems to have wanted an honest listener without bossing; Asif thanked Irawati 'for not bossing me' and laughed once the train came.

grounding: A sibling turns to an adult sibling for comfort and honesty; Irawati shows up, keeps the confidence and leaves the old bossy role behind.

passage:
Three weeks after their father's funeral, Mei found Felix at the kitchen table sorting mail into neat piles and talking about forms. Mei's first thought was that Felix felt nothing. Felix, watching Mei cry over a cracked coffee mug, thought Mei was making a scene.

That evening Mei took a breath. "How are you actually doing? Not the paperwork. You."

Felix stopped stacking. "When I keep busy, I can stand it," Felix said. "When I stop, I hear Dad whistling in the garage."

They went through the photo box until midnight, laughing at Dad's terrible fishing hat. The house papers stayed in their folder. "We'll deal with them in a few months," Mei said. "When it's not so raw." Felix nodded and put the lid back on the box.

qa.q: Where did Mei find Felix three weeks after the funeral?
qa.a: Mei found Felix at the kitchen table, sorting mail into neat piles.

qa.q: Why did Mei first think Felix felt nothing?
qa.a: Felix was sorting mail and talking about forms, which Mei read as coldness; Felix's later words show that keeping busy is how Felix stands the grief.

qa.q: What did Mei do that helped the two understand each other?
qa.a: Mei asked how Felix was actually doing, went through the photo box together with Felix, and agreed to leave the house papers for a few months.

qa.q: How did Felix see Mei's crying over the cracked mug at first?
qa.a: Felix thought Mei was making a scene, showing that the two were misreading each other's way of grieving.

grounding: After a parent's death two siblings grieve differently and misread each other; Mei asks about coping, shares memories and delays settling assets.

passage:
Day one. Over dal, Naveen's mother mentions that Suraj's coaching fees were never paid because the money went to Naveen's master's degree. Naveen says little all evening and lies awake counting the years.

Day four. Naveen still hasn't spoken to Suraj. Calls go to "later." Suraj sends a meme; Naveen leaves it unanswered and feels worse each day. The distance is growing, and Naveen knows it.

Day nine. Naveen drives over and says it plainly: "The money for my degree came from what would have been yours. I should have seen it. I want to make it fair, and I want to hear what fair looks like to you." Suraj is quiet, then says, "Thank you for saying it. Let's work it out slowly." There is no huge gift. They agree to split next year's family costs differently.

qa.q: What did the money for Suraj's coaching fees go to instead?
qa.a: The money went to Naveen's master's degree.

qa.q: Why does Naveen leave Suraj's meme unanswered?
qa.a: Naveen feels guilty and worse each day, and avoiding Suraj feels easier than admitting it, though the distance grows.

qa.q: What did Naveen do on day nine that worked better than silence?
qa.a: Naveen said plainly where the money came from, offered to make it fair, and asked what fair looks like to Suraj instead of handing over a huge gift.

qa.q: How might Suraj have read the days of silence before the visit?
qa.a: Suraj may have felt puzzled or ignored, since a meme went unanswered; the honest visit gave Suraj a reason for the gap and a chance to reply.

grounding: Naveen took more than a fair share of family support, feels guilty, and acknowledges it honestly with a fair repair rather than silence or over-giving.

passage:
In the baby-clinic waiting room, Hansa held her daughter and stared at the queue for the weighing scale without seeing it. Three weeks of broken sleep sat behind her eyes. "Everyone says it gets easier," she told Arohi, the nurse who called her name. "I keep thinking I'm doing this wrong."

Arohi checked the baby's chart and said, "Doubt like this is common with a newborn. What would help most this week?"

Hansa thought. "Someone to take the night feed. And the laundry can pile up, honestly."

"Then ask for exactly that," Arohi said. "And if the low mood stays, come and tell us. We can help you find support."

That night Hansa asked her husband Dev to take the 2 a.m. feed and messaged her mother to bring dinner. The dishes stayed in the sink.

qa.q: Who did Hansa tell that she keeps thinking she is doing this wrong?
qa.a: She told Arohi, the nurse who called her name.

qa.q: What is Hansa worried about?
qa.a: Hansa worries she is doing something wrong with her newborn, worn down by three weeks of broken sleep.

qa.q: What concrete help did Hansa ask for, and what did she let go of?
qa.a: She asked Dev to take the 2 a.m. feed and her mother to bring dinner, and she let the dishes stay in the sink.

qa.q: How might Arohi see Hansa's doubt?
qa.a: Arohi treats it as common with a newborn rather than as failure, and invites Hansa to come back if the low mood stays.

grounding: A new parent exhausted and doubting asks for concrete help, lowers housework standards, and is pointed to support if the low mood does not lift.

passage:
The baby had discovered the courtyard step, and Gargi's heart was already at the edge of it. A fierce wave rose in her: she wanted to wrap the baby in her shawl and keep them away from every step for ever. Neelam, the neighbour shelling peas on the charpai, glanced up. "Let them try, Gargi. I'm watching too."

Gargi crouched a metre away, hands ready but not touching. The baby wobbled, gripped the edge, and slid down onto their bottom with a startled laugh. Gargi let out her breath in a rush.

That night she told her husband, "I want to keep them safe from everything. But maybe they also need to find out the world can be walked on." She still moved the sharp scissors off the low shelf. Safe first, and free where it was safe.

qa.q: Where was Neelam sitting when the baby found the step?
qa.a: Neelam was on the charpai, shelling peas.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling as the baby reached the courtyard step?
qa.a: A fierce wave of protectiveness; she wanted to wrap the baby in her shawl and keep them away from every step.

qa.q: How did Gargi balance safety and freedom?
qa.a: She crouched close with hands ready but not touching, let the baby try the step, and still moved the sharp scissors off the low shelf.

qa.q: How might the baby experience being allowed to try the step?
qa.a: The baby gets to grip the edge, slide down and laugh, a small success that can build confidence.

grounding: A new parent feels a fierce need to shield the baby and learns to keep them safe without letting fear steal their freedom.

passage: I'm Ritu, and my flat shares a wall with Madhav and Shankar, who have a four-month-old. Through the wall I used to hear laughter. Lately I hear a timetable: "It's your turn." "I did the last one." Last Sunday I met Madhav at the lift with a bag of nappies and eyes like paper. "We're fine," Madhav said, in the voice people use when they aren't sure. On Tuesday I noticed a list taped by their buzzer: night duties, Monday to Wednesday Madhav, Thursday to Saturday Shankar, Sundays shared. Underneath, in different handwriting: "Thank you for last night." I can't know what was said inside. But I heard laughter again on Friday, then one long, quiet talk on the balcony, the baby asleep between them.

qa.q: What was written under the list of night duties?
qa.a: Underneath, in different handwriting: 'Thank you for last night.'

qa.q: What might Madhav have meant by saying 'We're fine'?
qa.a: Ritu notes it was said in the voice people use when they aren't sure, so Madhav may be tired and unsure while hiding it, though Ritu cannot know for certain.

qa.q: What small changes could help a couple like Madhav and Shankar?
qa.a: A fair split of night duties, short planned moments to talk like the balcony conversation, and saying thank you out loud as the note does.

qa.q: How might Shankar have felt reading 'Thank you for last night'?
qa.a: Shankar may have felt seen for the effort, since the note thanks a night duty; it fits the laughter returning by Friday.

grounding: New parents bicker like co-workers on a rota; a neighbour sees a fair night-duty list, spoken thanks and a planned talk begin to repair the partnership.

passage:
The family had come to Trisha's flat for the naming ceremony, and the rooms were full of noise and steam. Between the aunties' loud conversations, Deepika, Trisha's mother-in-law, said, "Why is the baby not wearing socks? And feed on a schedule, don't let them sleep in your bed." Trisha's own mother added a different rule.

Trisha, a new mother, felt her jaw tighten, judged in front of everyone. She could have snapped. She could have gone to the balcony and stewed. Instead she said, "Thank you, Deepika. I'll try the socks."

Later, in the bedroom, she told her husband, "The socks make sense. The schedule we'll decide ourselves." He squeezed her hand. "Together." She carried the tea back out with a small smile.

qa.q: What did Deepika ask about the baby's feet?
qa.a: Deepika asked why the baby was not wearing socks.

qa.q: How did Trisha feel as the advice piled up?
qa.a: Judged; her jaw tightened, though she chose not to snap or stew.

qa.q: What did Trisha do with the advice she was given?
qa.a: She thanked Deepika, took the socks idea, and left the feeding schedule for her and her husband to decide.

qa.q: How might Deepika have meant the advice?
qa.a: Deepika probably offered it as care and experience, which is why a thank-you served better than a snap would have.

grounding: A new parent facing constant advice from parents and in-laws feels judged, thanks them, keeps what helps and decides the rest with a partner.
